title: Can your grandfather's diet shorten your life?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain epigenetics: how chemical "methyl tags" switch genes on and off without changing DNA itself, turning the epigenome into a kind of software over the genome's hardware. They cover examples from honey bee queen development (royal jelly and the dnmt3 gene), agouti mice whose coat color and weight shift with methylation and with maternal B vitamin diet, and the Swedish Överkalix famine records linking grandparents' feast or famine to grandchildren's lifespan. They discuss the Angelman and Prader-Willi syndromes as imprinting examples, PTSD-like cortisol changes in children of mothers pregnant during 9/11, and how methyl tags may fade over a few generations. They also cover possible therapies (such as the drug azacitidine for leukemia), the effects of smoking and cocaine, the Human Epigenome Project, Bruce Lipton's controversial claims, and a listener mail segment about Sarah, a young fan with a blog.

entities.name: Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children

segments.title: Opening banter and Darwin vs. Lamarck
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on genetics and set up Darwin's theory of natural selection, the moon orchid and hawk moth anecdote, and Lamarck's giraffe idea as a precursor to epigenetics.

segments.title: Epigenome as software
segments.summary: Josh uses a hardware and software analogy: the genome is hardware and the epigenome tells cells what to do and when. Cells share the same DNA but differ by which genes are tagged on or off.

segments.title: Methyl tags as gene switches
segments.summary: Methyl tags, small chemical groups, attach to genes and block proteins from activating them, acting like a light switch that silences genes and can physically change how the genome is packed.

segments.title: Honey bee queens and royal jelly
segments.summary: Worker bees and queen bees share DNA; royal jelly adds a methyl tag to the dnmt3 gene in queen larvae, switching off the default worker pathway and allowing queen traits to develop.

segments.title: Agouti mice and diet
segments.summary: Agouti gene experiments in mice show that methylation status changes size, weight and coat color. Feeding pregnant mothers B vitamins produced thin brown offspring, while mothers on a normal diet produced fat yellow ones. Intermediate methylation produced spotted coats.

segments.title: Environment, nature vs. nurture, and inheritance
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how environmental factors such as diet, stress and exercise can affect children and grandchildren through epigenetic changes, framing this as a possible answer to the nature versus nurture debate.

segments.title: Swedish famine records and grandparents
segments.summary: Dr. Lars-Olov Bygren's study of nineteenth-century agricultural records from an isolated Swedish town found that grandchildren of grandfathers who experienced feast and famine within a year lived on average about 32 years less.

segments.title: Imprinting: Angelman and Prader-Willi syndromes
segments.summary: The hosts describe Angelman and Prader-Willi syndromes, caused by a missing piece of DNA whose effect depends on which parent it came from, a form of gene imprinting. They also mention the PBS documentary The Ghost in Your Genes.

segments.title: Methyl tags, egg and sperm, and PTSD
segments.summary: Methyl tags are normally cleaned during egg and sperm formation, but not all are removed, so some can be passed down. A study of women pregnant during 9/11 found their babies had lower cortisol, and hosts speculate about PTSD inheritance and mouse studies of maternal care.

segments.title: Reversibility, therapies, and the Human Epigenome Project
segments.summary: Methyl tags may fade after a few generations (fruit flies, mice, and an estimated three or so in humans). Hosts discuss epigenetic drug therapies for cancer and leukemia, the effects of smoking and cocaine, and the scale of the Human Epigenome Project.

segments.title: Bruce Lipton and the limits of the hype
segments.summary: Hosts discuss Bruce Lipton's claims that the mind can alter the epigenome, placebo effect and spontaneous remission, and note that some critics call him a quack while stress reduction may be a more plausible explanation.

segments.title: Resources and further reading
segments.summary: Hosts recommend the University of Utah epigenetics website, the PBS documentary, and the HowStuffWorks article on how epigenetics works.

segments.title: Listener mail: Sarah's blog
segments.summary: A listener mail from Sarah, a young fan now thirteen, shares her birthday news and her blog about Australian commercials. The hosts read her email and sign off with a Sound of Music farewell.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give the show's contact address and sign off, with a closing sponsor line.
